# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Building Permits Survey (BPS)
Description: The Building Permits Survey (BPS) provides national, state, and local statistics on new privately-owned residential construction. Data are available monthly, year-to-date, and annually at the national, state, CBSA (formerly MSA), county and place levels.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Building Permits Survey comprehensively. Let me start with several searches.I have solid foundational material. Let me gather more on the data's economic significance, access methods, and any preservation-related concerns.I have gathered comprehensive information from primary sources (Census Bureau, Federal Register/OMB clearance documents, HUD, The Conference Board, and third-party tools). Here is the full report.

---

# Research Report: Building Permits Survey (BPS)

## 1. Verification of Your Description

Your description is **accurate**, with minor elaborations worth noting:

- **Title**: Correct — "Building Permits Survey (BPS)," published by the U.S. Census Bureau.
- **Scope**: Correct — new **privately-owned residential** construction only (nonresidential permit data were discontinued in 1995; publicly-funded housing and HUD-code manufactured homes are excluded).
- **Geography/Frequency**: Correct — data are released monthly, year-to-date, and annually at national, Census region/division, state, CBSA (Core Based Statistical Area, formerly MSA), county, and permit-issuing place levels. Note that *preliminary* monthly data are only available at the national and regional levels; full geographic detail comes with the revised and annual releases.
- **Additional detail**: BPS collects both the **number of housing units authorized** and the **valuation of construction**, broken down by structure type (1-unit, 2-unit, 3–4 unit, and 5+ unit buildings).

---

## 2. Publisher and Stewardship

**Publisher**: U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce — specifically the Residential Construction Branch within the Economic Directorate (Manufacturing and Construction Division). Website: `census.gov/construction/bps` (also `census.gov/permits`).

**Related collections** (now combined administratively as the "Building Permits Survey Program"):
- **Form C-404** — "Report of Building or Zoning Permits Issued for New Privately-Owned Housing Units" (the core monthly/annual survey; OMB Control No. 0607-0094)
- **Form C-411** — "Survey of Residential Building or Zoning Permit Systems" (annual canvass to maintain the universe of permit-issuing jurisdictions; OMB Control No. 0607-0350). Per a February 2024 Federal Register notice (89 FR 9120), these two clearances were consolidated into one.

**Contact for data requests**: Residential Construction Branch, 1-800-845-8244, MCD.RCB.BPS@census.gov.

**Downstream redistributors** (important for preservation and access redundancy):
- **HUD Office of Policy Development & Research** — State of the Cities Data Systems (SOCDS) Building Permits Database (interactive query tool + CSV downloads)
- **HUD Open Data portal** (ArcGIS) — residential construction permits by county
- **NAHB (National Association of Home Builders)** — Housing Permit Data Portal
- **Center on Rural Innovation (CORI)** — open-source R package `cori.data.bps` (county-level, 2000–present)
- **FRED** (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) — national permits time series
- Academic mirrors and data commons (e.g., Data.gov catalog entry)

---

## 3. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Statutory authority**: Title 13, United States Code, **Sections 131 and 182**, which authorize the Census Bureau to conduct this collection.
- **Response obligation**: **Voluntary** for respondents — the survey is authorized (mandated) by law for the Census Bureau to conduct, but local permit offices are not legally compelled to respond. This is a notable and sometimes misunderstood point.
- **Confidentiality**: Title 13, Section 9(b) **exempts data customarily provided in public records from confidentiality rules**. Because building permits are public records, Census can publish place-level detail that would be suppressed in most other surveys.
- **Regulatory designation**: Building permits data feed two **Principal Federal Economic Indicators (PFEIs)** designated by OMB — *New Residential Construction* and *New Residential Sales*. This designation carries heightened release-schedule and data-quality requirements and signals the data's systemic importance to economic policymaking.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act**: The collection operates under OMB clearance with periodic renewals and Federal Register comment notices (most recent consolidation notice: February 9, 2024).

---

## 4. History

The BPS has one of the longest lineages of any U.S. statistical series:

- **1889** — The U.S. Geological Survey conducted the first federal collection of building permit data, using it to compare use of wood, brick, stone, and concrete against raw material availability near urban areas (~200 cities; no housing unit counts).
- **1920** — Congress requested data on new housing to address post–World War I housing shortages. The **Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS)** took over and built the first building permit reporting system, collecting the number and value of new housing units for the first time.
- **1920s–1930** — BLS published annual data for 257 of 287 cities with 25,000+ population; in 1930 it introduced a uniform mail-in reporting form.
- **1954** — BLS established the first formal permit-issuing universe and sample design.
- **1959** — Responsibility transferred to the **Census Bureau**. A canvass identified ~3,000 additional permit-issuing places (universe ~10,000), and the basic design still in use was established: a subset of places reports monthly; the rest report annually. **1959 is the start of the modern continuous series.**
- **1984** — Decision made to update the universe and monthly sample once per decade (universes: 1984, 1994, 2004, 2014).
- **1995** — Nonresidential permit data collection discontinued (historical nonresidential and demolition files, 1980–1995, remain available via special customer packages).
- **2011** — Online reporting option introduced for respondents.
- **January 2022** — Major methodology change: the monthly tabulation switched from a **probability (representative) sample to a cutoff sample** — all jurisdictions averaging 6+ permits/year over the prior three years report monthly; remaining places (~1% of activity) report annually only. This effectively eliminated sampling error from monthly estimates going forward.
- **January 2023** — The target universe shifted from a fixed decennial basis to an **annually updated universe** (~19,900 permit-issuing places), allowing faster coverage of newly incorporated or newly permitting jurisdictions.

---

## 5. Methodology in Detail

**Universe**: All ~20,000 permit-issuing jurisdictions in the U.S. (the "Active Governments File"), maintained via the annual C-411 canvass. The survey covers roughly 95% of all new residential construction; permit-free areas (some rural jurisdictions) are out of scope.

**Collection**: Local permit offices report by mail, online (since 2011), or via established electronic file-transfer arrangements (~625+ places historically; many states report on behalf of localities).

**Sampling/reporting structure**: Slightly less than half of jurisdictions report monthly; the remainder report annually. Since 2022 the monthly panel is a cutoff sample rather than a probability sample. Pre-2022 monthly estimates carry sampling error (a ~9,000-place stratified sample with certainty selections for large metro areas, small states, and cooperative reporters; non-certainty places sampled at 1-in-10 and weighted ×10).

**Imputation and nonresponse**: Monthly estimates include imputed activity for non-reporters and non-surveyed places. Historical unit response rates ran ~71% monthly / ~81% overall (2017 figures); the annual target is 80%+.

**Revision cycle**:
- *Preliminary* — released ~12th–17th workday after month-end, in the New Residential Construction press release (national and regional only; part of the PFEI).
- *Revised monthly* — ~17th–18th workday; adds state, CBSA, county, and place detail.
- *Final annual* — first workday of May the following year; all counties and places; prior-year monthly figures benchmarked to annual totals.

**Seasonal adjustment**: National/regional series published both unadjusted and at seasonally adjusted annual rates (SAAR).

---

## 6. Data Content and Structure

**Variables**: For each geography and period — number of buildings and number of housing units authorized, plus total permit valuation, by structure type: 1-unit, 2-unit, 3–4-unit, 5+ unit. Form C-404 also collects geographic coverage changes and, since recent clearances, supplemental detail on residential permits valued at $2 million+ (site address, building type) — though that detail is not in the public tables.

**Identifiers in place/county ASCII files**: survey date (YYYYMM; annual files use YYYY99 or YYYY), FIPS state and county codes, Census place codes, MCD codes, CSA/CBSA codes, a six-digit BPS place ID, central-city flags, footnote codes, and historical population fields. Full record layouts are documented in PDF technical documentation at `www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/bps/`.

**Formats**: Excel workbooks (U.S./region/state/CBSA, 2019–present); comma-delimited ASCII text files for state, CBSA, county, and place levels; historical text files (1995–2019 for state/MSA). Notably, **BPS is not part of the main Census API** — bulk ASCII/Excel files are the primary machine-readable route, which matters for data scientists building pipelines.

**Time coverage**: Continuous since 1959 (national/state/MSA); annual county and place data from 1980; monthly place-level from 1988; SOCDS monthly preliminary from 2001, monthly final from 1997.

---

## 7. Typical Users and Use Cases

Documented users (per Census Bureau and OMB clearance justifications):

- **The Conference Board** — building permits for new private housing units are one of the ten components of the **Leading Economic Index (LEI)**, because construction activity typically leads other economic production.
- **Federal Reserve Board** — analyzes national/regional economic conditions; housing's sensitivity to interest rates makes permits closely watched by monetary policymakers.
- **Bureau of Economic Analysis** — BPS data feed the **Residential Fixed Investment component of GDP**.
- **Census Bureau (internally)** — inputs to **annual population estimates**, which drive allocation of federal funding and resources to local governments.
- **HUD** — evaluates housing programs; maintains SOCDS for housing supply analysis.
- **Financial institutions** — mortgage demand estimation.
- **Private industry** — homebuilders (e.g., NAHB), building materials producers and retailers, market planning, site selection, investment analysis.
- **Local governments and planning commissions** — growth monitoring, infrastructure and service planning.
- **Academics and policy researchers** — housing supply elasticity studies, zoning and land-use regulation research (permits are the standard proxy for regulatory stringency's effect on construction), gentrification and development pressure analyses, and YIMBY/housing-abundance advocacy scorecards.
- **Journalists** — housing shortage coverage, metro-level construction rankings.

---

## 8. Benefits to the Public

1. **Unique coverage**: The OMB clearance states plainly that BPS is **the only source of statistics on residential construction for states, counties, and smaller geographic areas**. No private or other federal dataset replicates sub-state permit coverage nationally.
2. **Early-warning economic signal**: Permits precede starts, completions, and sales by months, making them among the timeliest indicators of housing-market and broader economic turning points.
3. **Public accountability**: Because it measures *authorization* activity of local governments, the data enable citizens and advocates to compare jurisdictions' housing production — a cornerstone of modern housing-policy debates.
4. **Resource allocation**: Indirectly shapes the distribution of hundreds of billions of dollars via population estimates.
5. **Transparency by design**: The public-records exemption in Title 13 §9(b) allows unusually granular publication (down to individual permit offices) without disclosure-avoidance suppression.

---

## 9. Limitations and Caveats (for data scientists and librarians)

- **Permits ≠ construction**: Authorization does not guarantee a unit is started or completed; the companion **Survey of Construction (SOC)**, partially funded by HUD, tracks starts/completions. Permit-to-start lag and non-starter rates vary cyclically.
- **Coverage gaps**: Areas without permit requirements (~5% of activity) are excluded; manufactured (HUD-code) homes are excluded.
- **Methodology discontinuities**: Treat January 2022 (cutoff sample) and January 2023 (annual universe updates) as series breaks for small-area analysis. Pre-2022 monthly estimates require sampling-error treatment; post-2021 estimates are effectively census-of-large-places plus imputation.
- **Imputation prevalence**: Both monthly and annual data may contain imputed values for non-reporters; the published micro-data blend reported and estimated figures.
- **Voluntary response**: Declining cooperation among local offices is a standing data-quality risk acknowledged in OMB filings.
- **Geographic instability**: CBSA delineations change with each decennial census; historical MSA files use period-appropriate boundaries — crosswalk carefully.
- **Nonresidential history**: Separate product (CD-ROM/ASCII customer package, 1980–1995) for nonresidential, additions/alterations, and demolition data.

---

## 10. Preservation Considerations

For preservationists and data librarians, key points:

- **Primary canonical sources**: `census.gov/construction/bps/` (web), `www2.census.gov/econ/bps/` and `www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/bps/` (bulk files and technical documentation). These are plain-text and PDF — highly preservable formats, but organized in legacy directory structures that warrant full-mirror capture.
- **Redundant copies to harvest**: HUD SOCDS, HUD ArcGIS open data, NAHB portal, the `cori.data.bps` R package (which bundles cleaned county data), FRED, and Data.gov metadata records.
- **Identifiers for cataloging**: OMB Control Nos. 0607-0094 and 0607-0350 (being consolidated); forms C-404 and C-411; legal cite 13 U.S.C. §§131, 182; PFEI designation.
- **Documentation to preserve alongside data**: methodology pages, record-layout PDFs (place/county/state/MSA ASCII documentation), universe history (1959–2023), and methodology-change announcements (Nov 2022 and Feb 2023 notices) — without these, the series breaks are indecipherable.
- **Release cadence risk**: monthly revised files are overwritten/superseded; annual May releases finalize the prior year. A preservation strategy should snapshot monthly vintages, not just annual finals, since vintage economic data are themselves research objects.

---

## Key Sources

- Census Bureau BPS portal, About, Methodology, FAQ, and Historical pages (census.gov/construction/bps/)
- Federal Register, 89 FR 9120 (Feb. 9, 2024) — OMB clearance consolidation for the BPS Program
- OMB Information Collection Request, OMB No. 0607-0094 (omb.report)
- HUD PD&R Edge, "Navigating HUD's State of the Cities Data Systems Building Permits Database" (huduser.gov)
- The Conference Board, LEI component descriptions and technical notes
- Census Bureau ASCII file documentation (www2.census.gov)

I'll research the current risk landscape for the Building Permits Survey, focusing on events since January 2025.Key context emerging. Let me check the ICR status, staffing tracker, and whether any 2025 disruptions affected BPS specifically.# Risk Assessment: Building Permits Survey (BPS)

**Assessment date context:** Research reflects conditions as of October 2026, covering the period since January 2025.

---

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence reviewed:**
- The Census Bureau's BPS portal continues to host current Excel files (2019–present) plus historical ASCII/text files going back to 1959 (national/state/MSA), 1980 (county/place annual), and 1988 (place monthly), along with complete technical documentation and record layouts (`www2.census.gov/econ/bps/`, `census.gov/construction/bps/historical.html`).
- The only alterations found are **documented, transparent revisions**: the 2022 annual files were revised and re-released in May 2024 (incorporating corrected New York City data and restored Puerto Rico estimates — which *added* geography), and historical Excel tables were migrated from .xls to .xlsx in February 2024 for accessibility — a format update, not a removal.
- Final annual 2024 data released on schedule May 1, 2025; final annual 2025 data released May 14, 2026 with full geographic detail (state, CBSA, county, place, island areas).
- Redundant copies exist at HUD SOCDS, HUD Open Data, NAHB, FRED, and in the open-source `cori.data.bps` package.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** No historical files or data elements have been removed; prior-cycle data remain accessible, and the one re-release event (2022 vintage) was corrective and well-documented.

---

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence reviewed:**
- **ICR status:** OMB Control No. 0607-0094 (Building Permits Survey Program, consolidating forms C-404 and C-411) is **active, expiring 05/31/2027**, and Census published a 60-day renewal notice in the Federal Register on **October 1, 2026** (91 FR 62465, comments due Nov. 30, 2026) — renewal is proceeding ahead of expiration, not lapsed.
- **Publication disruptions:** The October 1 – November 12, 2025 lapse in appropriations halted all collection and processing for the October 2025 reference period. Census published a formal PFEI recovery plan; New Residential Construction releases were delayed and combined reference periods (the Jan. 8, 2026 release contained September data; Feb. 18, 2026 contained November; Apr. 29, 2026 contained February). The 2025 annual BPS release slipped from the customary first workday of May to May 14, 2026.
- No termination of collection or publication; the time series was preserved with no permanently missing reference periods.

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** Typical/intended publication dates were missed and releases delayed over a roughly six-month recovery window — squarely matching the Moderate definition. Mitigating factors: the ICR is active with renewal underway, delays were caused by a funding lapse rather than policy choice, and the series remained continuous.

---

## Data Quality

**Evidence reviewed:**
- No policy-driven reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency. The February 2025 imputation methodology change (division/large-state factors instead of regional factors) was a refinement announced in advance, not a degradation.
- However, the shutdown recovery plan explicitly **shortened collection windows** (e.g., from 10 to 7 business days) and condensed review stages — a documented, if temporary, pressure on response completeness and analysis.
- The producing agency has lost an estimated **15% of staff since FY24** and over 1,000 employees, with a Commerce IG finding of inadequate strategies for staffing gaps; respondent cooperation for this **voluntary** survey was already a standing concern in OMB filings (historical unit response ~71–81%).
- Construction indicators relying on field representatives missed September 2025 collection entirely (this affects companion starts/completions data more than BPS itself, which is mail/online).

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** Quality dimensions are currently maintained, but there are credible *emerging* risks: compressed collection windows during recovery, severe agency-wide staffing attrition, and reliance on voluntary respondents during a period of institutional strain. Not High, because no actual reduction in granularity, timeliness, or frequency has been adopted as policy.

---

## Statutory Context

**Evidence reviewed:**
- BPS is authorized under **Title 13 U.S.C. §§131 and 182**, explicitly named on the survey's forms, burden statement, and web pages.
- The data feed two OMB-designated **Principal Federal Economic Indicators** (New Residential Construction; New Residential Sales) and are required inputs to BEA's GDP estimates (Residential Fixed Investment) and Census population estimates used for federal fund allocation.
- Per the OMB clearance itself, BPS is **the only source of sub-state residential construction statistics**; no alternative federal or private collection could substitute (HUD, NAHB, and FRED all redistribute Census data rather than collecting their own).
- Caveats: Title 13 *authorizes* rather than explicitly mandates this specific survey, and response is voluntary — but the rubric's "No Known Issue" tier explicitly accommodates named authorization plus no substitutes and federal-program dependence.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** Explicit statutory citation, no substitutes, and deep embedding in mandatory federal programs (GDP, fund allocation) make statutory risk minimal.

---

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence reviewed:**
- The Census Bureau has lost **more than 1,000 staff** since January 2025 (The Census Project, June 2025) — an estimated **15% staffing decline since FY24** (American Statistical Association, "The Nation's Data at Risk 2025").
- **Leadership turnover:** career Deputy Director/acting Director Ron Jarmin was replaced on September 19, 2025 by George Cook, a political appointee; at least five division/office chiefs departed in early 2025; the Director position has lacked a confirmed appointee.
- A government-wide hiring freeze (with only partial waivers), early-retirement/separation offers, and a Commerce policy requiring Secretary-level approval of contracts over $100,000 (3,000+ request backlog) have constrained operations.
- Funding: FY2026 enacted at $1.49B — above FY2025 ($1.385B) but $186M below the request; the Current Surveys and Programs account that funds BPS fell to $319M, ~3% below FY24/25 levels. Budget cuts alone do not reach rubric thresholds.

**Finding: High Risk.** Two independent High-tier triggers are met at the publishing agency: **1,000+ staff lost** and **leadership removed**. Caveat: publicly available figures are agency-wide; division-level (Manufacturing and Construction Division) staffing losses are not separately disclosed, so the specific BPS team's condition is uncertain — but the rubric's absolute headcount and leadership criteria apply at the agency level.

---

## Policy

**Evidence reviewed:**
- **No BPS-specific adverse actions since January 2025:** no Presidential-Action-driven ICR, no negative policy notes on the survey pages, no changes to what is collected. The only methodology change (imputation, Feb. 2025) was announced in November 2024 and is content-neutral.
- Housing supply data aligns with stated administration priorities (housing affordability), reducing targeting risk.
- **However:** the FY2026 President's Budget explicitly proposes to **"reorganize the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, and the Census Bureau,"** with details still undisclosed — a pending structural change to the statistical system that produces BPS.
- The agency has also demonstrated willingness to make abrupt, lightly-explained changes to other collections: cancellation of a 2026 Census of Governments classification survey, unannounced delays to the Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey, and postponement of 17 planned 2020 census assessment reports (NPR, April 2025).

**Finding: Moderate Risk.** Nothing targets BPS content directly, but there are *proposed or pending changes* (the statistical-agency reorganization) and a demonstrated pattern of abrupt collection changes elsewhere at the agency — matching the Moderate definition. Not High, because no Administration-priority-driven change to this specific collection has occurred.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

| Category | Level |
|---|---|
| Historical Data Availability | **No Known Issue** |
| Future Data Availability | **Moderate Risk** (shutdown-driven delays; ICR active, renewal underway) |
| Data Quality | **Moderate Risk** (emerging risks from staffing losses and compressed collection windows; no adopted reductions) |
| Statutory Context | **No Known Issue** (13 U.S.C. §§131, 182; no substitutes; PFEI/GDP dependence) |
| Staffing and Funding | **High Risk** (>1,000 staff and ~15% lost agency-wide; leadership removed/replaced by political appointee) |
| Policy | **Moderate Risk** (pending statistical-agency reorganization; pattern of abrupt changes to other surveys; nothing BPS-specific) |

**Overall interpretation:** The BPS dataset itself is intact, continuously published, legally well-anchored, and uniquely valuable — its *content* is at low risk. The meaningful risks are **institutional**: severe workforce attrition and leadership instability at the Census Bureau, demonstrated publication fragility during the 2025 shutdown, and a pending reorganization of the federal statistical system. For preservation purposes, the highest-value actions are mirroring the full historical ASCII/Excel archive and technical documentation from `www2.census.gov/econ/bps/` now (while it is complete), capturing monthly release vintages, and noting the redundant HUD/FRED/NAHB copies as fallback access points.
